title: Rachel's English: General American Pronunciation & Connected Speech
author: Rachel Smith
evaluation: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (5/5) — Gold Standard for General American Pronunciation

the_4_american_t_sounds.environment: At the start of a word or stressed syllable (e.g. *time, return*), or in a consonant cluster like /st/, /tr/ (*stay, train*).
the_4_american_t_sounds.mechanic: Clear air burst / puff of air released from the alveolar ridge.

the_4_american_t_sounds.environment: When T falls between two vowel sounds and the second syllable is unstressed (e.g. *water, city, better, butter, get it*).
the_4_american_t_sounds.mechanic: The tongue tip quickly strikes the alveolar ridge once without building up air pressure. Sounds identical to a quick Spanish single 'r'.

the_4_american_t_sounds.environment: At the end of a word when followed by a consonant sound, or before /n/ (e.g. *fitness, button, written, that book, wait for*).
the_4_american_t_sounds.mechanic: Air is stopped completely in the vocal tract or at the vocal cords, but NOT released.

the_4_american_t_sounds.environment: Commonly dropped after 'N' in casual conversational American speech (e.g. *internet* -> 'innernet', *twenty* -> 'twenny', *center* -> 'cenner').

common_reductions.example: I want to go -> I wanna go
I can do it -> /aɪ kən duː ɪt/ (Unstressed)

mouth_mechanics.vocal_placement: American English resonates in the chest and throat, giving it a rich, resonant acoustic quality, compared to British head/nasal placement.
